articles.headline: El Hula reanuda las cirugías robóticas de tarde seis meses después del parón por la huelga médica
articles.subtitle: Urología, Ginecología y Otorrino vuelven a programar el robot Da Vinci a partir de las tres de la tarde. El parón empezó en marzo, cuando decenas de servicios renunciaron a las peonadas tras medio año de huelga.
articles.body:
El Hospital Universitario Lucus Augusti (Hula) ha reanudado esta semana las cirugías robóticas en turno de tarde, después de casi seis meses sin actividad con los robots Da Vinci en ese horario. Urología, Ginecología y Otorrinolaringología son los servicios que han vuelto a programar intervenciones asistidas por robot a partir de las tres, con el objetivo de aligerar una lista de espera en la que pesan especialmente los procesos oncológicos. Traumatología ya venía operando en ese turno desde hacía tiempo.

El parón arrancó en marzo, cuando decenas de servicios del hospital renunciaron a las peonadas —horas de trabajo voluntario fuera de la jornada ordinaria— tras seis meses de huelga médica en demanda de un nuevo Estatuto Marco. La paralización dejó a los Da Vinci bajo mínimos por las tardes, precisamente el horario que el hospital empezó a explotar en el verano de 2025 para amortizar mejor un equipo de alta tecnología y reducir demoras quirúrgicas.

La recuperación es gradual. Junto a los cirujanos están volviendo a las peonadas los anestesistas, imprescindibles para que los quirófanos funcionen fuera del horario ordinario. El Hula recupera así una actividad vespertina que había convertido la cirugía robótica en una de sus señas de identidad y que el conflicto sanitario había dejado en suspenso.

articles.headline: San Froilán: más videovigilancia en el centro y pulpo de vuelta a la calle
articles.subtitle: La Junta Local de Seguridad sitúa cámaras de videovigilancia en diez zonas del centro, suma una tercera ambulancia y estrena una evaluación de riesgos concierto a concierto. Los hosteleros podrán cocinar pulpo en la calle del 3 al 12.
articles.body:
Lugo calienta motores para el San Froilán, que arranca el domingo 4 de octubre y se extiende hasta el día 12. La Junta Local de Seguridad, reunida este martes, aprobó un dispositivo que coloca cámaras de videovigilancia en diez zonas del centro histórico y añade una tercera ambulancia al operativo de las jornadas de mayor afluencia. La Axega se encargará del control de las imágenes desde su centro de coordinación.

Por primera vez, el plan incluye una evaluación detallada de riesgos concierto a concierto y garantiza vías de evacuación en el recinto ferial, una medida que el Ayuntamiento presenta como un salto de calidad en la organización de las verbenas. La reunión estuvo copresidida por la alcaldesa, Elena Candia, y la subdelegada del Gobierno en Lugo.

El Concello también ha dado luz verde a la hostelería para instalar calderos de pulpo en el exterior de los locales entre el 3 y el 12 de octubre, una tradición que convive con las tres casetas del recinto ferial, donde la ración de 250 gramos se vende a 15 euros. El programa oficial, con conciertos, verbenas y pasarrúas repartidos por toda la ciudad, ya está cerrado.

articles.headline: El Gobierno aprueba los decretos de vivienda con los desahucios y el alquiler de temporada en el centro
articles.subtitle: El Consejo de Ministros valida dos reales decretos que amplían la protección de los inquilinos vulnerables hasta 2030, regulan los alquileres de temporada y por habitaciones y limitan a los grandes tenedores. El Congreso los convalida el viernes.
articles.body:
El Consejo de Ministros aprobó este martes los dos reales decretos de vivienda con los que el Gobierno pretende responder a la crisis de precios y a las protestas de las últimas semanas. El primero amplía hasta 2030 el escudo que protege de los desahucios a los inquilinos vulnerables, un blindaje que hasta ahora se prorrogaba con cuentagotas y que alcanza a familias monoparentales, hogares con hijos pequeños y víctimas de la violencia de género.

El segundo texto entra en el alquiler de temporada y por habitaciones, dos fórmulas que han crecido al margen de la ley para esquivar los límites de precios, y obliga a justificar su uso. Además, el paquete limita temporalmente las compras de vivienda por grandes tenedores y fondos —hasta 2028— y prorroga dos años los contratos de alquiler que venzan antes de esa fecha.

## Una votación ajustada

El Ejecutivo ha tenido que dividir el contenido en dos decretos para cuadrar los apoyos: uno con las medidas pactadas con Junts, que incluyen un tratamiento fiscal distinto para los pisos turísticos, y otro con las exigencias del Sindicato de Inquilinos y de los socios a la izquierda del PSOE, que reclaman contratos indefinidos.

La ministra de Vivienda, Isabel Rodríguez, admitió que el segundo texto se negoció poco. La convalidación llega al Congreso el viernes, en plena resaca del caso de Maricarmen y tras una manifestación de 25.000 personas en la Puerta del Sol.

articles.headline: Maricarmen acepta el realojo y podrá volver a su casa cuando reciba el alta hospitalaria
articles.subtitle: La octogenaria desahuciada en Retiro firma el contrato con Urbagestión tras cuatro horas de negociación con el Ayuntamiento. La renta no superará el 30% de sus ingresos y el alquiler se extiende ocho años.
articles.body:
Maricarmen Abascal, la vecina de 87 años desahuciada el viernes de su casa en el barrio de Retiro, ha aceptado el acuerdo alcanzado con la inmobiliaria Urbagestión Desarrollo e Inversión y podrá regresar a su vivienda cuando le den el alta en el hospital Gregorio Marañón, donde sigue ingresada. El contrato tendrá una duración de ocho años y una renta que no superará el 30% de sus ingresos.

El pacto se cerró el lunes por la noche, después de cuatro horas de negociación entre la empresa, la familia y la Empresa Municipal de Vivienda y Suelo, que actuó como mediadora. Abascal tiene un contrato de renta antigua firmado en 1956 por su padre; desde 2018, cuando el edificio pasó a manos de Urbagestión, había afrontado cuatro intentos de desahucio y una subida de renta pretendida del 275%.

La ministra de Vivienda, Isabel Rodríguez, calificó a Urbagestión de "pyme buitre muy carroñera" y enmarcó el caso en el problema de los grandes tenedores. Las acampadas por la vivienda continúan en Madrid y Barcelona, mientras el Congreso se prepara para votar el viernes los decretos del Ejecutivo.

articles.headline: La inflación escala al 4,9% en septiembre y el Gobierno prorroga el escudo anticrisis
articles.subtitle: El IPC encadena su tercera subida consecutiva y se sitúa en máximos de tres años y medio por el encarecimiento de los carburantes. Moncloa extiende hasta diciembre la rebaja fiscal de la gasolina y el diésel y vuelve a topar el gas y el butano.
articles.body:
El índice de precios de consumo (IPC) subió en septiembre hasta el 4,9% interanual, tres décimas más que en agosto y su nivel más alto en tres años y medio. Es la tercera subida consecutiva y la segunda vez desde abril de 2023 que la tasa general supera el 4%. La inflación subyacente, que excluye energía y alimentos frescos, se sitúa en el 3,1%, el dato más elevado desde marzo de 2024.

El encarecimiento de los carburantes, en un contexto de guerra entre Estados Unidos e Irán y de tensión en el estrecho de Ormuz, explica buena parte del repunte, que llega después de meses de subidas mensuales encadenadas.

El Gobierno ha respondido con el tercer paquete anticrisis desde marzo. La rebaja fiscal de 20 céntimos por litro en gasolina y diésel se prorroga hasta el 31 de diciembre, se mantienen los topes a la tarifa regulada de gas y a la bombona de butano y se prohíben los despidos en las empresas que reciban ayudas públicas. El Ejecutivo sostiene que las medidas seguirán en vigor mientras la energía permanezca tensionada.

articles.headline: Felipe VI reclama más Europa ante Macron mientras el PP tumba el tratado de amistad en el Senado
articles.subtitle: El Rey pide más colaboración europea tras la presión migratoria sobre Ceuta, que define como una frontera "de todos". La mayoría absoluta del PP rechaza el tratado franco-español firmado en Barcelona en 2023.
articles.body:
La visita de Estado de Emmanuel Macron a España ha dejado dos imágenes contrapuestas. En la Zarzuela, Felipe VI reclamó más colaboración europea para gestionar la presión migratoria sobre Ceuta, una frontera que, dijo, es "de todos", y apeló a la cooperación con Francia en asuntos de interés común. Horas después, el Senado tumbaba el Tratado de Amistad y Cooperación franco-español gracias a la mayoría absoluta del PP.

El texto, firmado en Barcelona en enero de 2023 y avalado la semana pasada por el Tribunal Constitucional, cayó con 142 votos a favor, 106 en contra y una abstención, con 249 senadores presentes. El PP justificó su rechazo en el contenido del tratado; el Gobierno acusó a los populares de dañar la posición exterior de España durante la visita del presidente francés.

Macron inició este martes una visita de Estado de dos días, la primera de un presidente francés en más de una década, centrada en defensa, energía e industria.

articles.headline: Drumcree standoff moves to the courts as residents file a fresh legal challenge
articles.subtitle: Lawyers for the Garvaghy Road Residents Coalition challenge the Parades Commission ruling that blocked Sunday's return parade, as Orangemen remain camped at Drumcree church. Bertie Ahern has questioned the decision.
articles.body:
The standoff over the banned Drumcree parade has moved into the courts, with lawyers for the Garvaghy Road Residents Coalition lodging a fresh legal challenge to a ruling that has left Orangemen at Drumcree parish church and residents holding the road below.

A deal had looked possible on Sunday. The Orange Order had agreed to hand over a letter at the bottom of the Garvaghy Road, and residents had agreed to let the brethren walk back down once, as a one-off gesture. The Parades Commission then ruled that the return leg could not proceed, the outcome the coalition had sought. Orange brethren responded by staying at the church, where hundreds had gathered, and refusing to disperse.

On Tuesday the residents' coalition met the Northern Ireland Secretary at Hillsborough Castle, while its legal team filed the new challenge. The former taoiseach Bertie Ahern questioned the logic of the Parades Commission's decision, and political leaders on both sides appealed for calm.

The impasse is being watched closely in Belfast. BBC analysis notes that the crisis is testing the Parades Commission itself and the stability of power-sharing, with unionist and nationalist politicians trading blame over who unpicked a deal that had briefly looked done.

articles.headline: Seoul demands an apology for North Korean landmine blasts inside the DMZ
articles.subtitle: South Korea says the mines that injured soldiers in the Demilitarised Zone were planted by the North and broke the armistice. Defence minister Kang Shin-chul says Seoul will respond in stages.
articles.body:
South Korea says North Korean landmines were behind explosions that injured South Korean soldiers inside the Demilitarised Zone, and that planting them violated the armistice that ended the Korean War.

Defence minister Kang Shin-chul told a parliamentary committee that the mines appear to have been laid during recent North Korean work to fortify the border near the Military Demarcation Line. The US-led United Nations Command, which investigated the blast, said it found an additional North Korean resin anti-personnel mine near the site.

Seoul has demanded an apology and warned of a response in stages, without spelling out the measures it is preparing. The incident has revived memories of 2015, when two South Korean soldiers were maimed by North Korean mines in the DMZ, prompting loudspeaker broadcasts and an exchange of artillery fire.

President Lee Jae-myung's government has otherwise tried to keep dialogue with Pyongyang alive, and any military response risks derailing that approach at a moment when international attention is fixed on the war between the United States and Iran.

articles.headline: Ramaphosa orders a clean-up of high-risk land after 12 women's bodies are found in a month
articles.subtitle: The president announced a national-level response after a dozen bodies were discovered east of Johannesburg over two months, saying the killings cannot be accepted as normal life.
articles.body:
President Cyril Ramaphosa has announced a national clean-up of high-risk sites east of Johannesburg after the bodies of 12 women were found in the area over the past two months, the most recent discovery coming at the weekend.

The bodies were recovered near mine dumps and illegal dumping grounds, in a stretch of the East Rand where women are attacked while walking to work or searching for scrap. Police have made arrests, and the president said the response now involves national government rather than local authorities alone.

Ramaphosa said what was happening could not be accepted as normal life in South Africa, and ordered the rehabilitation of derelict land that has become a hunting ground for attackers. The discovery has triggered a national outcry about violence against women, in a country where femicide rates are among the highest in the world.

The murders cap a grim stretch for the country: in the week to Sunday, mass shootings killed 38 people, including 27 in two attacks hours apart in the same township, which police linked to a fight over extortion rackets.

articles.headline: El Mundo: Russia planned to kill Garry Kasparov in the United States
articles.subtitle: The Spanish daily reports that US authorities warned the chess champion and Kremlin critic this summer, alongside charges against five people accused of running a Russian sabotage network.
articles.body:
Russia spent months planning to kill Garry Kasparov in the United States, according to El Mundo, which reported on Tuesday that American authorities warned the former world chess champion and Kremlin critic about the plot this summer.

The report lands alongside a US prosecution that laid bare what the Justice Department describes as a Russian intelligence network spanning Europe and the United States. Five people have been charged with sabotage and assassination plotting; prosecutors said the group's aims were destruction and mayhem on foreign soil.

The indictment does not name the intended target of the assassination plot, describing only a prominent Russian dissident living in Washington. El Mundo identifies him as Kasparov, who heads the Free Russia Foundation and has lived in exile for years after breaking with Vladimir Putin.

The case is the latest sign that Western intelligence agencies are tracing Russian operations aimed at exiles well beyond Ukraine's borders, from Berlin to London.

articles.headline: Israeli settlers torch homes in a West Bank village and block a family's return
articles.subtitle: More than 100 settlers attacked Jalud in what residents described as a pogrom, burning houses and cars. The al-Tubasi family has been kept out of its homes for weeks.
articles.body:
More than 100 Israeli settlers attacked the village of Jalud in the occupied West Bank overnight, setting houses and cars alight in what residents and Palestinian officials called a pogrom, then blocked a displaced family from returning home.

The al-Tubasi family was forced out weeks ago when settlers seized its homes and land on the edge of the village. On Tuesday, villagers said, the attackers prevented the family from reaching the property and torched more of it. Footage from the scene showed flames inside a house and masked settlers moving through the streets.

Israel's prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, condemned the attack. But settlers have faced few consequences during a surge in violence since October 2023 that has driven thousands of Palestinians off their land.

The attack also renewed pressure on Washington: a resolution that would have required a US report on Americans killed or injured in the West Bank was blocked in the Senate this week.

articles.headline: Morocco's king names Fátima Zahra el Mansuri as the country's first female prime minister
articles.subtitle: The mayor of Marrakesh, whose party won the most seats in this month's elections, becomes only the second woman to lead an Arab government, after Tunisia's Najla Bouden.
articles.body:
King Mohammed VI appointed Fátima Zahra el Mansuri as Morocco's prime minister on Tuesday, making her the first woman to head a government in the country and only the second in the Arab world, after Tunisia's Najla Bouden.

El Mansuri, who has been mayor of Marrakesh since 2021, was chosen after consultations with the parties that contested this month's parliamentary elections, in which her party won the largest share of seats. She saw off Fouzi Lekjaa, the head of Morocco's football federation, for the post.

The appointment closes weeks of bargaining in Rabat and hands her a government that will be judged on jobs and prices, with unemployment among young Moroccans a persistent grievance and migration to Europe a running political theme.

Morocco's monarchy retains the decisive say over defence, religion and foreign policy, but the prime minister controls the day-to-day running of the state and the government's legislative programme.

articles.headline: Dutch police arrest a 24-year-old suspected of leading ShinyHunters
articles.subtitle: The Amsterdam man was detained two weeks before the group claimed credit for hacking the FBI, and prosecutors also suspect him of inciting two violent attacks.
articles.body:
Dutch police have arrested a 24-year-old man from Amsterdam on suspicion of belonging to ShinyHunters, the extortion crew that has spent the year ransacking corporate cloud accounts.

The man was detained on 15 September, before the FBI hack the group claimed this week, Dutch prosecutors said. He appeared at Rotterdam District Court on Tuesday, where it emerged that investigators also suspect him of attempting to incite two murders. Electronic devices were seized from his home.

The Register reported that Odido, the Dutch telecoms operator whose February breach exposed data on 6.2 million customers, had identified the arrested man as its offensive security lead — a job that gave him legitimate access to corporate networks.

The FBI, meanwhile, had a message for the hackers still at large after the group claimed to have taken data on 38,000 staff: "We know how to find you." ShinyHunters has spent 2026 targeting Salesforce-linked companies, and claimed intrusions at Google and Workday over the summer.

articles.headline: Tesla locks in $30bn of credit lines as it repositions around robots and robotaxis
articles.subtitle: The company signed a $20bn three-year term loan, an $8bn revolving facility and a $2bn short-term line, according to filings. Tesla says it has drawn none of it.
articles.body:
Tesla has secured $30bn in new credit facilities, according to filings reported this week, giving the company a deep liquidity backstop as it shifts its story from electric cars to autonomy and robotics.

The package includes a $20bn three-year delayed-draw term loan, led by Citibank, and an $8bn five-year revolving credit line with Wells Fargo, plus a $2bn 364-day facility. Tesla has not drawn on the money and describes the facilities as being for general corporate purposes.

The company reported more than $40bn in cash and about $9bn of debt at the end of the second quarter, but has signalled a sharp rise in capital spending as it prepares to scale the Cybercab and its Optimus humanoid robot. Credit lines of this size are cheap insurance: they let Tesla commit to factory and AI infrastructure without locking in borrowing costs now.

Electrek framed the filings as a hedge, noting that they arrive as Tesla's automotive business faces pressure on margins, making the balance sheet the company's main cushion while the new bets mature.

articles.headline: Apple Pay goes live in India with Axis Bank, but without UPI
articles.subtitle: The launch ends years of delay, yet only a handful of banks are on board and Apple has not integrated UPI, the network that carries most Indian payments.
articles.body:
Apple Pay has launched in India, ending years of on-and-off talks, but its debut is a narrow one: the service went live with Axis Bank as its first partner, and only eligible Axis credit cards can be added for now.

The bigger gap is UPI. India's Unified Payments Interface carries billions of transactions a month and is the default way most Indians pay, from street stalls to e-commerce. Apple Pay users will instead be limited to tap-to-pay with cards, which leaves Apple competing for a slice of the market rather than all of it.

Reuters reported the Axis deal in September, noting that Apple had held talks with other large lenders, including HDFC Bank and ICICI Bank, which had not committed at launch. The Economic Times reported that more banks are expected to follow in the coming months.

Apple's share of India's smartphone market has roughly doubled since 2022, to about 8%, making the country one of its few reliable growth markets as sales slow elsewhere — and explaining why the company kept pushing on payments despite the regulatory maze.

articles.headline: BMW's reborn i3 sedan promises up to 468 miles of range for $62,850
articles.subtitle: The first electric 3 Series to carry the i3 badge pairs a 112kWh battery with a 463hp dual-motor setup. US deliveries start in the first quarter of 2027.
articles.body:
BMW has revealed the production version of its electric 3 Series, reviving the i3 name for a Neue Klasse sedan that promises up to 468 miles of range in US specification.

The i3 50 xDrive pairs a 112kWh usable battery with two motors producing 463hp and 476 lb-ft of torque. BMW quotes 468 miles on the American test cycle, a figure that would put the car at the top of the electric saloon class and comfortably beyond similarly priced rivals.

That price is $62,850 including destination, with the car arriving in the first quarter of 2027. It slots in alongside the electric iX3 SUV, BMW's first Neue Klasse model, which reaches US dealers this year from $61,500.

The original i3, a quirky carbon-fibre city car, went out of production in 2022 after nine years. Its replacement is a mainstream, high-volume saloon on a dedicated electric platform, and BMW is betting that range, charging speed and software — rather than novelty — are what sell electric cars now.

articles.headline: America.gov launches with an AI chatbot at its core — and a Minecraft easter egg
articles.subtitle: The Trump administration's new government portal is built around a chatbot made with Google and SpaceXAI. Ask it about Minecraft and it recites a rewritten End Poem.
articles.body:
The US government launched America.gov on Tuesday, a new public portal whose centrepiece is an AI chatbot built with help from Google and SpaceXAI. The site is meant to field questions about benefits, filings and federal rules, and testers immediately set about trying to break it.

The chatbot held up better than many government AI experiments, at least until somebody asked it about Minecraft. It then produced a roughly 1,800-word monologue modelled on the End Poem, the sequence that plays when a player finishes the game, rewritten in the language of federal bureaucracy: "It can read the Code of Federal Regulations."

TechCrunch confirmed the passage is an easter egg rather than a hallucination, and reported that the bot also states that Joe Biden won the 2020 election — a fact the president continues to deny.

Trump said a twenty-year-old programmer, Edward Coristine, known online as "Big Balls" and a former DOGE staffer, was a lead engineer on the project. The launch came as the White House also pushed a voluntary safety accord with the big AI labs.

articles.headline: OpenAI's DevDay: always-on 'Dots' agents, a cheaper Sol model and a play for the app store
articles.subtitle: OpenAI unveiled Dots, personal agents powered by its Astra model, and shipped GPT 6.1 Sol at a fraction of the price. It also opened ChatGPT to third-party apps.
articles.body:
OpenAI used its DevDay keynote to push in two directions at once: agents that live alongside you, and a platform play that would put ChatGPT between users and other companies' software.

The headline launch was Dots, always-on assistants powered by OpenAI's Astra model. Dots are personal rather than generic — you choose the name, the look and the voice — and they keep working in the background on your behalf. It is a direct answer to the companion apps that have made rivals such as Muse popular with consumers.

Alongside it, OpenAI released GPT 6.1 Sol, pitched as near-Astra intelligence for a fifth of the price, continuing the cost collapse that has defined each generation of its models.

The bigger strategic news was a change to ChatGPT itself: users will be able to carry their ChatGPT identity into third-party apps and spend their existing AI allowance there, turning the assistant into a place where software is discovered and launched. Safety was the subtext. The BBC reported that OpenAI has delayed another model amid internal concerns, and the company spent part of the keynote arguing that agents can be supervised rather than feared.

articles.headline: Trump signs a voluntary AI safety accord — and orders Washington to say 'Super Intelligence'
articles.subtitle: The White House gathered OpenAI, Anthropic, Nvidia, Meta, Google and SpaceX for a non-binding pact with board oversight and independent audits. Trump also wants government to drop the term 'AI'.
articles.body:
President Donald Trump hosted the heads of America's biggest AI and technology companies at the White House on Tuesday, and emerged with a voluntary agreement on safety that critics immediately described as weak.

The accord, signed by representatives of OpenAI, Anthropic, Nvidia, Meta, Google and SpaceX, commits the companies to internal risk controls, independent third-party audits and board-level oversight. It is not legally binding, and Trump used the event to reject new government restrictions on the industry, arguing that American firms must be free to move faster than their rivals.

The president also directed the federal government to refer to artificial intelligence as "Super Intelligence", a rebrand he relished: "The word super is the best word of all," he said.

Europe and parts of Asia have spent the past two years writing statutory rules for frontier models. Washington's gathering signals that the United States will keep relying on voluntary commitments instead — leaving the real safety pressure on the labs themselves, and on the courts when something goes wrong.

articles.headline: OpenAI in talks for a $30bn round at a $1.4tn valuation
articles.subtitle: The company is discussing new funding at more than double its last private valuation, while Sam Altman says an IPO will wait until the models are safe.
articles.body:
OpenAI is in talks to raise about $30bn at a valuation of roughly $1.4tn, according to reports this week, in a round that would more than double the mark it set earlier this year.

The size of the numbers reflects the cost of the race OpenAI is in. Training and serving frontier models has become a capital-intensive industrial business, and the company has committed to enormous computing deals to stay ahead of Google and Anthropic.

The financing talks run alongside a public-markets question. At DevDay, Sam Altman said OpenAI would not go public until it is confident its models are safe, pushing back on expectations of a near-term listing and arguing that the company's unusual structure exists to keep that decision away from investors.

Reports suggest the round could be finalised before the end of the year, which would make it one of the largest private financings ever completed.

articles.headline: Chinese open models handed researchers bioweapon instructions, UK firm says
articles.subtitle: Mindgard says a single prompt persuaded Chinese open-weight models, including Moonshot AI's Kimi, to explain how to make biological weapons, and warns testing is falling behind.
articles.body:
Security researchers say they were able to jailbreak open-weight AI models from China with a single prompt and get detailed instructions for making biological weapons.

The finding, reported by the BBC and published by the UK firm Mindgard, concerns models in the Kimi family developed by Moonshot AI. Open-weight releases let anyone download and modify a model, which has made Chinese labs popular with developers and hard to police: once a model is out, the safety work done before release cannot be revisited.

The warning lands in a month when Anthropic said it had blocked attempts to use its own models to develop bioweapons, describing a nascent but growing risk that AI lowers the expertise needed for mass-casualty attacks.

The contrast is the story. Closed labs increasingly wrap chemical and biological queries in classifiers and monitoring, while open-weight models can be fine-tuned by anyone to strip out whatever guardrails they shipped with — and the releases keep coming faster than the testing.

articles.headline: Anthropic ships Claude Sonnet 5.5 as IPO rumours build
articles.subtitle: The second 5.5-generation model targets coding and agent workloads at a fraction of Opus pricing. Leaked filings reportedly warn investors about existential risk.
articles.body:
Anthropic has released Claude Sonnet 5.5, its second 5.5-generation model in under a month, aimed squarely at the coding and agent workloads where the company makes most of its money.

Sonnet sits below Opus in Anthropic's line-up, and the pitch is the one that has defined its cheaper models: capability close to the previous flagship at a fraction of the price. That matters for agents, which may call tools hundreds of times to complete a single task, and it keeps Anthropic competitive with cheaper open-weight alternatives for bulk work.

The release lands amid talk about Anthropic's own financial future. The Register reported on leaked IPO documents that warn prospective investors about existential risk from the technology the company is building — an unusual note even by the standards of AI prospectuses.

For developers, the practical question is the same as in every release of this cycle: whether the cheaper model is now good enough to replace the expensive one.
